metadata.title: Relationship between digital game experience and problem-solving performance according to a PISA framework

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a recruited convenience sample of 6th-grade students from a single school in Taoyuan County, Taiwan, and administered questionnaires and computer-based tasks over five weeks. The methods report SPSS analyses (t-tests, one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlations, and linear regressions) but do not describe the use of complex survey weights or any sampling-weight variables. Because the design is a small, school-based recruitment rather than an international representative ILSA sample, standard PISA-style student weights are not discussed; the manuscript therefore provides no weight variable name or weighting procedure. No replicate-weight approach (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is mentioned, and the analysis appears to treat observations as unweighted individual-level data.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not analyze PISA cognitive achievement scores with plausible values; instead, it uses author-designed and game-based performance scores (e.g., a 71-point computer-based problem-solving score and a 40-point Cataroundasia process score) plus self-regulated learning questionnaire scales. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based ILSA achievement scales, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript reports exclusions for incomplete data, absences, computer crashes, or withdrawal, but it does not document a formal missing-data handling method (e.g., imputation vs. complete-case rules) for remaining missing questionnaire/task items, so the missing-data strategy is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: A total of 290 sixth-grade students (ages 11–12) were recruited from nine classes at one school in Taoyuan County, Taiwan. The final sample included 267 students after removing unusable surveys due to incomplete data, absences, computer crashes, or project withdrawal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving (6th grade, Taiwan)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Experienced vs inexperienced: t = −3.224, p < .001; one-way ANOVA across experience groups: F(4,262) = 3.17, p = .014; regression of performance on process stages: R = .544, R2 = .296, F = 27.555, p < .001; stage betas: representation & formulation β = .344 (t = 6.243, p < .001), monitoring & reflection β = .193 (t = 3.330, p = .001), planning & execution β = .126 (t = 2.161, p = .032), exploring & understanding β = .117 (t = 2.104, p = .036).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving data from 6th-grade students in Taiwan, the study leveraged Digital game experience, Self-regulated learning (total), and Problem-solving process (total) (with stage scores) to predict Computer-based problem-solving performance (0–71), finding that more digital game experience and higher problem-solving process—especially representation & formulation and monitoring & reflection—were associated with higher performance. This indicates that strengthening students’ digital game-related experience and training problem representation and self-monitoring skills may improve performance on dynamic, technology-mediated problem-solving tasks, though the evidence is correlational and based on a single-school convenience sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving (6th grade, Taiwan)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pearson correlations with computer-based problem-solving performance: self-regulated learning r = −0.165, p < .05; action control r = −0.158, p < .05; motivation and strategy: not significant (reported as no significant correlation).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving data from 6th-grade students in Taiwan, the study leveraged Self-regulated learning (total) and its subcomponents (motivation, action control, strategy) to predict Computer-based problem-solving performance, finding weak negative correlations for self-regulated learning and action control and no significant correlations for motivation and strategy. This indicates that self-reported self-regulated learning may not straightforwardly translate into better measured problem-solving performance in this setting, suggesting that future interventions should focus on observable process skills rather than relying solely on self-report scales, while noting that the study’s design and measurement may contribute to the unexpected direction.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving (6th grade, Taiwan)
main_findings.target_variable: Problem-solving process stages predicting dynamic vs static performance
main_findings.performance_metrics: Dynamic performance regression on stages: R = .508, R2 = .258, F = 22.808, p < .001; significant predictors: representation & formulation β = .276 (t = 4.892, p < .001), planning & execution β = .175 (t = 2.925, p < .01), monitoring & reflection β = .207 (t = 3.483, p = .001); static performance regression: R2 = .202, F = 16.587, p < .001; significant predictors: exploring & understanding β = .141 (t = 2.384, p < .05) and representation & formulation β = .343 (t = 5.855, p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving data from 6th-grade students in Taiwan, the study leveraged the four problem-solving process stages to predict Dynamic vs Static problem-solving performance, finding that representation & formulation was the strongest predictor in both cases, while dynamic problems additionally depended on planning & execution and monitoring & reflection and static problems depended more on exploring & understanding. This indicates that instruction should differentiate process training by problem type—emphasizing planning and real-time monitoring for dynamic/technical tasks and observation-based understanding for static/non-technical tasks.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving (6th grade, Taiwan)
main_findings.target_variable: Problem-solving process stages predicting technical vs non-technical performance
main_findings.performance_metrics: Technical performance regression: R = .509, R2 = .259, F = 22.899, p < .001; significant predictors: representation & formulation β = .287 (t = 5.090, p < .001), planning & execution β = .162 (t = 2.722, p < .01), monitoring & reflection β = .196 (t = 3.302, p < .01); non-technical performance regression: R2 = .174, F = 13.806, p < .001; significant predictors: exploring & understanding β = .125 (t = 2.085, p < .05) and representation & formulation β = .332 (t = 5.576, p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 framework-based computer problem-solving data from 6th-grade students in Taiwan, the study leveraged the four problem-solving process stages to predict Technical vs Non-technical performance, finding that representation & formulation was again the strongest and most consistent predictor, while technical contexts also required planning & execution and monitoring & reflection. This indicates that digital literacy supports for technology-mediated problem solving should explicitly train students to plan actions and monitor feedback loops, whereas non-technical tasks may benefit more from strengthening observation and problem representation.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a PISA 2012 framework to design a computer-based problem-solving assessment and a separate Cataroundasia process task for 267 recruited 6th-grade students in Taiwan. It reports no machine-learning models; instead, it uses SPSS-based correlations, one-way ANOVA, and linear regressions to test relationships between digital game experience, self-regulated learning, and problem-solving performance. Students with more digital game experience scored higher on the 0–71 computer-based problem-solving performance (ANOVA F(4,262)=3.17, p=.014; experienced mean 62.6 vs inexperienced 52.8; t=−3.224, p<.001). Problem-solving process stages significantly predicted overall performance (R2=.296), with representation & formulation the strongest predictor (β=.344, p<.001) and monitoring & reflection also significant (β=.193, p=.001). The study is limited by its single-school convenience sample, author-created measures, and the absence of PV-based ILSA scaling/weights; additionally, self-report self-regulated learning showed weak negative correlations with performance.
